message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Landlords must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• The Texas Property Code requires landlords to repair major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must give notice of non‑renewal at least 30 days before the lease ends. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without proper notice (usually 24–48 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • Ask for written notice of any planned entry. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • Report any discriminatory practices to the Texas Attorney General or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to repair, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure (notice, filing, court order).
• Common reasons: non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or landlord’s own use of the property. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, you can file a defense in court. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must respect your privacy and cannot harass or threaten you. | • Document any harassment and consider filing a complaint. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents. | • Get written permission if required. | | **Maintenance of Common Areas** | • Landlords must maintain common areas (hallways, elevators, parking lots) in a safe condition. | • Report hazards promptly. | ### How to Protect Your Rights 1. **Read the Lease Carefully** – Look for clauses on rent, deposits, repairs, entry, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written communication, and receipts help if disputes arise. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – Texas law specifies how much notice is needed for rent increases, lease changes, or entry. 4. **Use Written Communication** – Email or certified mail provides a paper trail. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you encounter a problem, contact the Texas Attorney General’s Office, local tenant‑rights groups, or a housing counselor. 6. **Consider Legal Counsel** – For complex issues (e.g., eviction, discrimination), an attorney can guide you through the process. --- #### Quick Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Housing** | Consumer complaints, tenant‑rights guides, and legal assistance. | | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on fair housing and landlord‑tenant laws. | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Free or low‑cost legal advice, mediation services. | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | National fair housing resources and complaint filing. | Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific aspect, such as how to handle a security‑deposit dispute or what to do if you’re facing eviction.
